It's February 10th 2012. You just got out of class for the day. You head to Family Video that has an attached Little Ceazers. You go in and grab a brand new copy of The Darkness 2 off the shelf and rent it for a week for $5. You pop into Little Ceazers next door and grab a Hot-N-Ready pepperoni for $5. You go home to your crappy college apartment and play D2 all night and crush that Hot-N-Ready like it was nothing. Didn't really get better than that.

It doesn't take you long to be pulled into the story. The Darkness 2 does a great job of immersing you into the feelings and thoughts of the main character, which is a rarity in modern day gaming. Often you are very disconected from the story and the emotions of the characters. Lately, the only other game I have played that did such a great job of pulling you in, emotionally, was BioShock Infinite.

Beyond the story, which while nothing especially impressive, what is there is enough and is well orcestrated. The most impressive feat is the game's ability to put you in the shoes of the main character and really doubt what is real and what is not real (in the game).

The gameplay is top notch though and if you enjoy shooters where you run from one area to the next and have to clear all the waves of enemies, then this is a game for you. The gunplay is fun and has impact and the tentacles are well implemented so that they are not overpowered and yet are still very fun and exciting to use. 
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=304584465
I found myself using primarily guns but definitely had to use my powers frequently to stay in the fight. I was glad though that the powers did not dominate the gameplay so that you simply use the powers when you feel the need and are not forced to constantly use the powers. In some games where you have powers they dominate the other gameplay mechanics to the point that you find yourself only using the powers and nothing else. Fortunately, this is not the case in the Darkness 2.
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=304361429

The graphics are not impressive or special, but they make up for what they lack in the style, which once you've played the game to completion the style will make sense. A lot of people were surprised when they first revealed the first gameplay video of The Darkness 2 because of the art style they had used. But there is a definite reason for it and it only further helps immerse you into the world of confusion that the main character is living in.
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=304361384
The soundtrack is great and the voice work is top quality. All in all, it is a very fun game with a decent story that manages to pull you in and leaves you desiring more.

Would definitely recommend giving this game a spin! It is a great purchase and a great experience to play through once or even twice! In addition there are even some co-op missions to further the experience, so if you have a friend to play it with it will add a few more hours of quality gameplay.

You know those games you have sitting in your collection for god knows how long, that you always overlooked and once you finally got around to it you wondered how you could have overlooked it for so long? Yeah this definitely is the case for me with Darkness 2. 

I am guessing it was on sale so I picked it up at some point but needless to say I knew nothing about this game and never played the original. Usually sequels are not as good as the originals but if this is a lesser game the original must be the best game ever made! 

This game is a real gem, a must play if you like shooters and are looking for something a bit different. I wont spoil any of it other than to say it was not at all what I expected (in a good way) and even the cut scenes kept me watching when in 90% of games I will skip them if they ramble on too much. 

Graphically the game has a really cool art style that looks good and ran very smoothly on my PC. Sounds are also of a high standard as is the voice acting. 

There really is not much to complain about here, though if I had to look for something to whinge about I did find it annoying that your ability to heal and picking up dropped weapons are both bound to the E key. Which meant that during intense fights I found myself accidentally picking up weapons with no ammo instead of eating hearts to heal (you will see what I mean) and that did get annoying. 

But overall this game has really intense gun play, great voice acting and dialogue that isn't destroyed with political correctness and the entire game is really well done. 

Highly recommended

It is a shame the first game is not available for PC because it follows the story right where the first instance left it; a direct continuation on a story-driven game is kind of a big deal and the 'Previously: on The Darkness' doesn't even quite explain the full happenings of the first game. If you're going to play on this, I would suggest watching a 'Let's Play' of The Darkness 1 at least; sadly that's the best solution for it right now.

The game is good and can be considered a sort of a cult classic. The superpowers we are so used to get automatically while playing a game (immortality as we can just try levels again, regenerating health, ability to take bullets without flinching) are explained by canonical reasons. The delivery of most lines is good and there is a certain character that makes finding the collectibles all worth it: his fun narration of what every single Relic is is masterful.

While your character is a powerhouse, he's not against slouches and the game was a challenging experience, more so because you can get punished by killing your opponents in the simplest or easiest ways while if you go for flashy or risky maneuvers you can get more powerful if you don't mind having to retry a few times more while you learn the limits of where you can take cockiness to.

The story is good, since the source material that is based on is well-written, no surprise there; the portrayal of it is what is wonderful. You have this incredible power, but they can accurately portray it as a double-edged sword, a curse that is so deceitful that even when it tries to help you have no idea if it's merely playing you or screwing you over. I loved that kind of trip and mental games it made me go through.

The campaign is alright, but it also has a co-op mode where you can take completely different characters with unique powers each - talk about going the extra mile - for completing challenging levels that sort of explain what was happening on the background of the story while Jackie, the main character, went on his usual rampages. Some more milage for the game if you want to take it; all in all, it's a bit on the shorter side but not so much that you wouldn't feel it's worth it. Again, I hoped there were more entries of The Darkness, either the first game or even a continuation of this one as the ending is... very open for one.

-Didn't run into a single bug

So yea id get this game when its on sale if you want to play it, unless dropping 30 bucks for ~5 hours of gameplay is worth it to you.

Released almost a decade ago, "The Darkness II" continues to shine as a testament to the idea that a great game never truly ages. In an era of rapidly evolving gaming standards, this supernatural shooter manages to not only hold its ground but also stand out as an exceptional experience.

The heart of "The Darkness II" is its captivating narrative. It blends the dark, gritty world of crime drama with supernatural horror elements, creating an unforgettable storyline that keeps you engrossed from start to finish. The compelling character of Jackie Estacado, who's struggling to contain the ancient and malevolent force known as "The Darkness" within him, is a central figure in this gripping tale.

One of the game's key strengths lies in its gameplay, where gunplay meets supernatural abilities. The integration of The Darkness' powers into combat is both seamless and electrifying. You can summon dark tendrils to tear through your enemies, impale them, or even devour their hearts to replenish your powers. These dark and unique abilities elevate the gameplay to a whole new level.

Visually, "The Darkness II" has aged remarkably well. The graphic novel art style gives the game a timeless quality, providing a captivating and visually distinct look that remains impressive even by today's standards. The character designs, environments, and overall presentation hold up admirably.

It's not just nostalgia that keeps "The Darkness II" relevant; it's the combination of its compelling narrative, immersive gameplay, and striking art style that makes it stand out. This is a game that manages to capture the essence of an enduring classic while remaining appealing to a new generation of gamers.

In conclusion, "The Darkness II" is a supernatural shooter that proves that good game design and storytelling never go out of style. It's a title that has aged gracefully, offering a captivating experience that is just as enjoyable today as it was when it first graced our screens. If you're seeking an immersive and unique shooter with a compelling narrative, don't hesitate to dive into the dark and thrilling world of "The Darkness II." It's an experience that continues to shine brilliantly.

Darkness II is the FPS game with controversial visuals, action mechanics and story plot. Definitely not for "everyone's tastes". I remember playing it right after the release, and I remember that I was far from satisfied with it back then. So... I let the time wipe out part of my memory, to be able to play this game anew, to make myself a detached and detailed judgment about it. And here it goes.

[i]Hello, darkness, my old friend. I've come to talk with you again.
Because a vision softly creeping, Left its seeds while I was sleeping,
And the vision that was planted in my brain still remains within the sound of silence.[/i]

Can't see a review about this game as complete without that reference to Simon and Garfunkel's well-known song. Because, well, this game is actually full of references. The story of the Darkness games and comic series is, for the most part, a long innuendo to the so-called "dark part of the human nature".

Lust, Gluttony, Greed, Despair, Wrath, Pride, Envy - we'll meet them all in Darkness II, impersonated and spilled all-around - any way you like it. Alas, pop-culture phenomena like comic books and video games ain't exactly known for really deep immersion and scrutiny of those sins of mankind and their role in history. While the game is eager to show you so many symbols and allusions of the fight between good and evil, light and dark in the soul of man... It is not actually going any deeper than that. To put it blandly, Darkness II was not made for people looking for some philosophy. 

Darkness II is the game that allows you to tear your foes apart, literally. It is a game about ripping the spinal from the man and then eating his heart. It is a very specific type of FPS, somewhat similar to Bullet Storm game, for example, thanks to the additional mechanics that are giving you more Exp points for the more varying kills. More Exp you'll gather, more additional ways of destruction you'll unlock: the ability to run akimbo with different guns, all-penetrating shots, a swarm of bees to keep your enemies busy when they, you know, trying to swarm around you... And so on. The shooting mechanic itself is the coin of two sides: for one, the enemies and surroundings are quite responsive for your shots, and that is good. For another side, though, the aiming is made for consoles, even on the hardest difficulty you just need to click at least somewhere close to the enemies to hit them. And forget about ballistics and all that nonsense - the game is half-slasher, what ballistics to you need? Just point and click, and don't forget to ripe some spinals for bonus ammo and health replenishment.

The cell-shading visual style might look a bit off, but it serves at least one purpose: the game still looks fresh enough. So I think that cell-shading works as a preservative, saving the game from the time. What is really wonderful about Darkness II is the sound work: background music, voicing (especially Johnny Powell talking about those collectible artefacts) and all that stuff. Shooting mobsters by the sounds of "Black Betty" or Ton Loc's "Wild Thing" was really fun as well. Too bad that the second half of the game is much less music-infused.

Speaking of other details, such as level design, the depth of background provided, the overall expression from the game... it is well-made. Solid piece of work. There are no big code work issues (except some GPU driver troubles, check the forums if you're Red), no game-breaking glitches... It's a nice game if you like the gameplay where you're supposed to wreak havoc and unleash your inner darkness into this already dark world, and if you don't mind the supernatural story with walking symbols of human sins for all main characters, starting from your "hero". You're also supposed to accept that almost every woman in that game will be killed, because of your actions. And that all story plot is following the trivial comic book rules. And that you'll know all the twists in that plot long before you'll see it.

All in all, I'd give Darkness II 7.8 points out of 10. But! I still don't like it. And I still not really suggest it to everyone. It's a decent FPS/slasher game for those who don't actually care about "why?" or "what for?" but rather only for "how?"

It's not a "good game" if you're, say, have "lawful good" or "Paragon" alignment. Or if you're under the age of 16, and can't control your hormones at least somehow. Or all of that combined. Let the light come forth!

When The Darkness was first released back in 2007, it wasn’t primarily marketed as a comic book adaptation. As a result, only a small portion of players actually knew it was based on a comic series. I was already familiar with Marc Silvestri’s work (Cyber Force, Wolverine, Witchblade), and after watching an interview with the Swedish developers at Starbreeze during the Games Convention, I knew there was no way I could pass on The Darkness. Right next to BioShock and Assassin’s Creed the game immediately landed on my Must-Play-07 list. Another reason for my excitement was that I had already played The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay by the same studio, which had impressed me with its dense atmosphere, innovative mechanics and cinematic presentation. Compared to Riddick, which came out in 2004, The Darkness received slightly lower review scores from critics but for me personally, it resonated much more deeply and left a far greater impact.

Looking back now, I can hardly explain why it took me thirteen years to once again step into the shoes of the bearer of darkness, Jackie Estacado, and his embark on another brutal journey of revenge. But one thing’s for sure, even after all these years, it didn’t let me down. The story is intense and tragic, a rollercoaster ride between madness and guilt. Yes, the mafia elements are a bit cliché at times, but its strong narrative structure and sense of direction makes you forget about that. The visual style has been slightly altered, giving the game a more comic-like appearance, something I welcomed and think was executed well. The many hand-drawn objects and assets add a great deal to the game’s charm. Compared to the first part, there are a few moves that I had missed back then, for example you can now tear car doors off vehicles and use them either as shields or throwing weapons. I also had a lot of fun picking up rebar or pipes and pinning enemies to walls with a well-aimed throw. And while the new finishing moves bring a breath of fresh air, it’s still a little shame that the Creeping Dark ability from the first game is no longer available here, or that you have to unlock the Black Hole power first. The thing I appreciated the most, however, was that Mike Patton returned as a voice actor for the game. Anyone who knows the extraordinarily talented vocalist of bands like Mr. Bungle, Fantômas or most famously Faith No More, will hopefully also know that Mike’s performance as the voice of the Darkness is absolutely and tremendously incredible.

What brings me to one of my favorite things, the sound design and music, both of which manage to blend technical precision with carefully crafted artistic direction. First of all credit where it’s due, all the other voice actors also did a great job. Brian Bloom, for example (Call of Duty, Dead Space, Wolfenstein), and Stephanie Frame, who replaced Kirk Acevedo and Lauren Ambrose, both delivered convincing vocal performances. Certain sound effects like the brutal tearing of enemies, the hiss of the demonic tendrils, or the formation of the Black Hole are strikingly intense and almost physically tangible, the weapons sound heavy and distinct. But even beyond the action-packed sequences filled with cinematic sound, the game maintains its dark tone through a thoughtful mix of ambient layers, atmospheric sounds and ethereal notes that keep the tension and immersion alive throughout. It’s not unusual to find yourself, after a chaotic stretch of combat or a cutscene, suddenly drifting into some sort of in-between world or vision, and the sound follows you there. Deep strings, drones and synth pads build an ominous, floating soundscape, joined by vocal textures, breathing noises and distant echoing voices. Even a broken ceiling lamp spitting out occasional sparks adds beautifully to the environmental storytelling. What surprised as well, was the sheer number of well-known songs scattered throughout the game appearing in the most unexpected moments and triggering waves of nostalgia. More than once, I caught myself saying: Hey wait a minute, it's that one song by... (Deftones, Type O Negative, Stereo MCs, In Flames, The Flamingos, Dean Martin, Thievery Corporation...).

Alongside the main story, there are also side missions featuring four additional characters, each equipped with unique weapons and abilities. These can be played solo or in online co-op mode. And once again to my surprise, it's a lot of fun, but mostly thanks to the character J.P. Dumond, who can hurl enemies into the air with his voodoo staff and summon black holes. I’ve enjoyed it so much that I’ve already replayed all of those missions several times, always finding myself coming back to them, still I know sooner or later it will all come to an end. Digital Extremes, the studio behind The Darkness II, once expressed interest in making a sequel. However, it apparently never materialized due to disappointing sales figures. There were fan initiatives, petitions and social media groups trying to convince 2K Games and Top Cow to greenlight a continuation. But despite the passion behind the movement, the numbers just weren’t there. Without a larger community, media attention or notable industry voices, such efforts rarely have an impact. A revival like that would need a coordinated campaign with thousands of supporters, ideally paired with a comic event or even a Witchblade crossover. And even then, it would all rise or fall based on the strength of the new concept.

What? You want a short version of how I imagine it? Alright, since you’re asking so nicely. In my opinion, a proper concept would need to aim for at least 2+ million copies sold. And not only should long-time fans lose their minds when the first trailer drops, it should be so breathtakingly impressive that everyone takes notice and a well-deserved hype starts building. How would that even work, you ask? Well, simple: The Darkness III would have to be a visually and mechanically overwhelming blockbuster, something that feels like a full-on power trip with almost completely destructible environments. On top of that, every single light source could be disabled, because the darker it gets, the more powerful you become. The Serpent Heads/Demon Arms wouldn’t just tear enemies apart in brutal and creative ways, even simple strikes could shatter bones, leaving arms limp and enemies crawling helplessly on the ground. I’d also find a clever way to integrate a number of the actual Darkness comics into the game, not only to highlight its comic origins but also to give newcomers an accessible gateway into that world. Ideally, Mike Patton would return as the voice of The Darkness. Maybe the devs could even reuse some of the old recordings, or better yet, let Patton collaborate with a group of selected musicians and composers to create an exclusive soundtrack for the game. That could only turn out amazing. Yeah… that’s roughly my short version. Until then, it remains what it is, potential waiting to rip everything apart.

The Darkness 1 is my favourite game of all time, no contest. It has charm, unique artistic design, a soul-tingling soundtrack, visceral melee animations, and some of the most emotional writing I've ever seen in a game, as well as heartfelt side missions to add to that further. The small section of the city you're in feels like yours, lived in, ripe to explore. There's hidden depth to certain word choices from key figures that make you go "oh ♥♥♥" when you realise it later, especially when it comes to this sequel and its twists.

Originally the core parts of this game's plot were intended to be melded and released into the first game. (There's even some unreleased voice lines that REALLY tease at this game's ending, hiding in the first game's files!) So the question that remains is, does this one hold a candle to the perfection of the first? I'd say mostly yes. The focus on stronger combat does not overtly distract from a narrative that is still dark, vengeful, and ultimately heart-wrenching.

I still pray for a remaster of the first, and a third installment to continue from that dang cliffhanger we've been left with.

The Darkness II:

This is the second Steam account that I have owned The Darkness II on so before you look at my time played and say "You haven't played through it", I have. I've played through the entire game multiple times.

First and foremost, this is the most underrated game on Steam. That's why I voted for The Darkness II for the "I Thought This Game was Cool Before it Won an Award" award.

One major complaint that I have about The Darkness II is how short its campaign is. It's not difficult to beat it in around six hours. That might sound a little disappointing compared to its predecessor's much longer runtime, it's really not that bad. If you were to cut out the first game's mundane side missions and mindless wandering around the labyrinthine city and the subway tunnels below it, both games would be about the same length. I don't know about you, but I'd much rather have six incredible hours of gameplay than twelve mediocre hours with a few good parts thrown in.

There are four characters you can choose from, and their unique skill trees and Darkness weapons make each of them worth checking out. There's Inugami, a swordsman who has to kill to satiate his cursed katana lest it take his soul; a Scotsman named Jimmy Wilson, who has a love for the drink and a fondness for splitting skulls with an axe; a voodoo shaman named JP Dummond, who wields a powerful staff; and Shoshanna, who gets up close and personal with her double-barrel shotgun. None of them are particularly relatable characters, but they're all solid, and their unique weapons and skill sets offer some incentive to play through Vendettas more than once. That's a good thing though because the mode only takes a few hours to complete.

The Darkness II is everything I wanted a sequel to The Darkness to be. It's almost excessive in its violence, the combat is addicting, the hand-drawn Graphic Noir art style is gorgeous, and underneath it all is a game with a heart and a truly interesting story. Jackie's a supremely messed-up individual, but I still love him because of all the stuff he's willing to go through in order to save Jenny. If you're looking for any of these things, The Darkness II won't disappoint.

The Darkness II mixes crime drama and supernatural horror and handles both fairly well. Since the first game is not available on Steam, I played this one without any knowledge of the previous story. Even so, it was easy enough to understand what was happening. 

The game explains the important details along the way, and the voice acting helps during key scenes. The story is quite straightforward and some characters do not get much development, but the campaign moves along at a steady pace.

Combat is where most of the game's attention is focused. The mix of shooting and supernatural abilities gives more options during fights than a standard FPS. As the game progresses, new abilities become available and add more variety to encounters. 

The levels are mostly linear, with little reason to explore away from the main path, but there is always another fight around the corner. The dark environments and lighting suit the overall tone of the game.

Overall, the campaign is short, but it does not overstay its welcome. The comic book visual style helps the game look different from many other shooters, and the music and sound design match the darker atmosphere. The story and level design are fairly simple, but the combat remains the main highlight throughout the game.

Considering how society works today, there's not many games bieng released that could compare to the perfect blend of action and sadism that The Darkness II features. While there are many games out there that may be even better, this game in it's essence is something else. Imagine you're playing MAFIA II, but your protagonist carries what seems to be a symbiont similar to Venom from the Spider-Man series. Yeah, that's a good example. The first and second game are based on the comic series, sadly only the sequel is available on PC. This said, this game is brutal, full of action, possible replayability if you want to unlock everything, and lots of guts and blood. Let us resume it all by points and facts:

✨ PLOT (SPOILER ALERT): The story puts you in the shoes of Jackie Estacado, who is the host of a awakened cosmic-magical entity called "The Darkness", which is passed on through his bloodline once the host reaches adulthood. He is also the head of the Mafia currently. This is not mentioned on the game, since this is the sequel. But you probably need to know this, in order to understand the game more.  Even so, once you get into the game, you will have a tough time connecting some stuff. So I advise you all investigate the comic series plot after beating it, and or play the first game as well. Do keep note tho, the games are different from the comics. Anyways, following his awakening and all that happened in the first game, Jackie gets an unexpected visit and assault from The Brotherhood, the evil guys and secret society who wants to gain control of The Darkness and take over the world. They do some pretty edgy and immoral stuff throughout the game, leaving Jackie with no option but to put a stop to it all, struggle against The Darkness and it's fight to control it's host, and finally save his sexy beloved in a Dante's Inferno sort of way. That's pretty much it, and the game is quite short but will keep you invested. There are two endings, so save often in each chapter/level or at the start of each. The game series got cancelled, so do not expect any resurrection of it later in life. 

✨ LORE AND DIALOGUE: There's a lot of dialogue in this game casually when stuff is calm and you're free to speak to characters. It's always interesting to hear their stories, jokes, or other stuff. I did hear every single thing while recording the game to Youtube (I do that a lot). Interacting with the world and characters, for me is the absolute lively experience in videogames. But what's dope, is the actual lore related to the history of The Darkness. There are collectibles called "Relics", when found this dude called Johnny will explain the backgrounds of these items to you in a fully-voiced way. I did not find them all sadly, but hearing bro out made the game even more interesting for me. So get all those if you can!

✨ CONTROLLING THE DARKNESS: In the game you will be able not only to wield firearm variety but also slash, gnaw, destroy, slice, and murder your enemies with the help of The Darkness itself and the Darkling (A manifestation of Jackie's subconscious created by The Darkness, you will probably love the guy).  As you progress in the story and battle your way, you will gain points from kills and consuming hearts which you will use to upgrade a multi-tree of abilities and buffs. You will also be able to use the Darkling in some ways and play as him. You will unlock attack and armor upgrades, ammo, synergy upgrades, and even different ways to kill the enemy in gruesome ways to gain resources. I did not unlock everything, but apparently there's a NEW GAME+ option, so this might be of interest for completionists.

✨ PERFORMANCE: Even after so long back when I played it on my laptop, this game ran flawlessly for me. Truly enjoyable and peak optimization. The animations were as smooth as I remember them, and man do I love this type of artstyle featured. I did not experience any lag, or stutter throughout the whole campaign. In fact, the game felt so comfortable and fast that my only issue was keeping up with all the action on the screen while executing combos and killing everyone. I did see some negative reviews claiming the game soflocks you on modern setups and stuff, then again I've seen those in other games I already played just fine. So who knows what the issue is there, could be anything related to your PC. Did not come across any bugs or glitches, so I found my experience a satisfying trip. You can all check part 1 of my gameplay here, but don't overstay if you don't want to get spoiled much: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aR7rDUeJ9Ps&t=929s

As someone who has not played the first game, I came into this one not knowing what to expect - and was pleasantly surprised. The Darkness II proved to be an enjoyable ride from start to finish, well paced and not outstaying its welcome, and you will not be penalised for not playing the original (there is a "previously" video at the start to bring everyone up to speed).

Without giving away spoilers, you play as Jackie Estacado, out for revenge after an attempted hit with your awakened powers. The gameplay itself is naturally focused on your abilities (as an example, I found managing ammo for guns to be a constant pain, and that was with a high percentage of headshots) and the controls can be quite unintuitive at first - but this quickly passes. The upgrade system, which both augments existing abilities and adds new ones, also prevents the action from becoming monotonous. The Vendetta and Hitlist sections also add some extra meat to the game and help to substantiate some of the story (although they are best played after finishing the main storyline), and also allow some co-op play - which works surprisingly well.

With smooth, fast-paced gameplay, adequate controls (albeit controls that take some getting used to), a well optimised engine (not surprising given the game's age), and excellent characterisation - The Darkness II is a properly entertaining ride.

Embrace the Darkness - you won't regret it.

The Darkness II is one of those games that initially feels like it was made with one very simple objective: make the player feel powerful.

And honestly? It succeeds.

It's short, linear, has some rough edges, and features a few mechanics that will make you go "BRO WTF?!". But underneath all of that is one of the most satisfying combat systems I've ever played. You aren't just shooting enemies here - you're tearing them apart with guns, demonic tentacles, environmental weapons and supernatural abilities. And it is FUN!


[b]Combat - S-Tier[/b]

Let's start with the obvious: the combat is fucking sick.

The Darkness II does something I wish more games would do: YOU are the monster. You aren't some guy who occasionally gets a cool ability; supernatural power is the core of your arsenal and the entire system is built around letting you abuse it.

The guns are great too. There aren't many, but they have serious f-ing punch. This isn't pew-pew-pew - shooting someone feels like you're actually BLASTING them. Dual-wielding feels AMAZING without sacrificing aim precision.

The game is generous with ammunition. You're constantly getting enough ammo to actually use your weapons and have fun instead of hoarding every bullet like a priceless artifact. Coming from games where you're practically begging for three handgun rounds (RESIDENT EVIL VILLAGE) - this was pure BLISS.

My biggest complaint is headshot detection. Seeing a clean cross-map blast to someone's face get a generic "kill +10" is underwhelming and wastes ammo. It's not game-breaking, but it definitely takes some satisfaction out.



[b]The Darkness - Awesome[/b]

This is where the game really separates itself. The Darkness abilities are incredibly fun, and the upgrade system rewards you with meaningful improvements instead of meaningless stat increases:

Road signs become sawblades.
Pool cues become spears.
You can get black holes and THROW THEM AT PEOPLE!!!
You can tear out people's hearts and eat them.
You can imbue the Darkness into your firearms.

Utility abilities like the flies keep the arsenal diverse. The game constantly gives you Essence to upgrade, encouraging you to experiment with the ridiculous crap you've been given. The executions in particular are f-ing INSANE. It's creative, violent, responsive and EXTREMELY fun.



[b]Enemies & The Light - Cool idea with a questionable execution[/b]

There are cool enemy concepts here, but inconsistencies start becoming noticeable. The Brotherhood using Darkness-powered weapons is a neat concept, but the rules feel contradictory—they can use Darkness weapons in full light without penalty, while a random f-ing lamp can one-shot you.

And speaking of light: those f-ing projector enemies... Holy sh. The concept is solid—light weakens you, forcing a tactical shift—but the execution gets really annoying. They drain your health extremely fast, hit you from absurd distances through cover, and hit detection for shooting light sources is spotty. You end up melted because apparently a flashlight became the strongest weapon in the game.

Constantly stopping to shoot lights hurts pacing. Darkness-shield enemies trigger a similar frustrating loop: shoot them, use your Darkness ability, try to grab them, miss, try again, and wonder what the game actually wants. Most issues stem from hit detection rather than bad concepts.



[b]Bosses - Probably the weakest part[/b]

Unfortunately, boss fights don't live up to the rest of the combat. There are only about four, and most follow the same formula: boss appears far away → teleports around → starts potshotting → you shoot the di in the face.

They aren't damage sponges, which I appreciate, but there are few interesting mechanics. After how creative the normal combat is, bosses feel surprisingly basic and like a missed opportunity.



[b]Level Design & Exploration[/b]

The game is very linear, moving through closed environments with obvious progression and loading transitions. For a 2012 action game, it works well. The art style holds up great, and there's only ONE main collectible type, placed naturally enough that you don't need to turn the game into a scavenger hunt. For a short linear title, I have little to no problem with the level design.



[b]Technical Issues[/b]

Playing at modern high framerates causes strange collision issues. Several times I got completely stuck in tiny spaces—underneath floorboards, vents, or geometry—and getting unstuck becomes an entire damn ritual:

Turn V-Sync on. Turn V-Sync off.
Try fullscreen. Try borderless.
Alt-tab.
Restart checkpoint.
Run into wall. Jump. Run-jump.
Pray.

Eventually you squeeze through. It happened three or four times—not constant, but annoying enough to mention.



[b]Story & Characters - Surprisingly Interesting[/b]

The unique mix of mafia drama, demonic supernatural power, and psychological horror is something you don't see often. The Brotherhood works well enough, though the game expects you to know the events of the original (unfortunate since it isn't on Steam). The recap is decent, but blind players might feel slightly confused. Still, the story carries you through, backed by EXCELLENT voice acting across the board (- Everyone has a fahkin Jerseh accent thouh, bouhss...).



[b]The Psychological Stuff[/b]

I particularly liked the psychological sequences. At first you think "this is obviously a dream-", then you're left questioning reality. Thankfully, the game doesn't pull the usual f-ing "IT'S ALL UP TO INTERPRETATION!!" ambiguous bullsh and refuse to commit. It gives you an actual explanation and commits to what's happening. I much prefer a story that actually knows what it wants to say. The twists surrounding Jenny genuinely caught me off guard.



[b]Characters[/b]

Jackie is a straightforward protagonist trapped between mafia life and a demonic curse. The Darkness itself is the star—creepy, manipulative, bloodthirsty, and clearly running its own agenda. Supporting mafia characters are enjoyable, though I wish the game made them feel more vulnerable; despite all the chaos, nobody around Jackie feels threatened, making them feel like invincible background assets.



[b]Length - short-ish, but not complaining[/b]

The campaign is only around 5-6 hours. And honestly? Good. I'd rather have a fantastic 5-hour game than a 5-hour game padded into a miserable 30-hour experience with meaningless objectives and repetitive encounters AS MOST ACTUALLY ARE. The Darkness II gets in, lets you tear people apart, tells its story, and gets the f--- out. Could there have been more? Absolutely. Would I have liked more? YES. But I'd much rather be left wanting another few hours than spend twenty hours wondering why developers haven't stopped yet.



[b]Completion & Extras[/b]

Vendetta/Hit List missions add extra scenarios to enjoy the combat. The achievement list isn't overly difficult, though forcing a New Game+ playthrough for 100% completion is a bit of a chore.



[b]Final Verdict[/b]

The Darkness II is damn good. Its combat is easily the highlight—one of the most creative and satisfying systems I've played. Guns, dual-wielding, supernatural powers, and brutal executions give you absurd freedom to obliterate anything in your path.

It has flaws: headshot hitboxes can be garbage, light mechanics disrupt the flow, bosses are underwhelming, and high framerates turn geometry into black holes. But none of that overshadows how much fun it is. The story is interesting, voice acting is great, and it finishes before it overstays its welcome.

I finished it wanting more rather than wanting it to end—and that's a pretty good problem to have.

[b]8/10[/b]

Darkness 2

There is something appealing about being a force of nature. Something driven by sheer will or in the most extreme cases, a disastrous anomaly. Stories like Punisher, Mad Max and The Darkness imbue a certain surreal appeal of being an antihero or in this case a force of nature that will wreak havoc at anything that comes along its path. Most of the time there is nothing you can actually do to reason with their sense of morality. Darkness 2 developed by Digital Extremes and publish by 2K is a thoroughly enjoyable force of nature romp and allows you to explore that sense of morality through Jackie Estacado eyes.

 It’s overall tightly paced and has some satisfying amid some repetitive game choices. The unique fatality system is interesting and gory but it gets somewhat repetitive after doing the same move for 90th time. In a lot ways, it sort of started the whole glory kills system seen in DOOM 2016. Darkness 2 starts off with a bang with Jackie Estacado now the big boss of the Franchetti crime family being ambushed by what seem like a rival mob at first but soon it becomes clear something is amiss. The story takes places two years after The Darkness with Jackie still reeling from the loss of his girlfriend Jenny Ramano. Jackie has tried to bury the darkness powers due to its violent nature and it preventing him from saving Jenny. When the ambush begins, Jackie is soon forced to unleash the darkness and face ensuing consequences that come after.  The story is told remarkably well, with colourful characters, secret societies, and excellent voice acting just like the previous entry. However it’s the graphics that sets a very different tone for the series with its cell shaded and comic book like graphics paying a much more faithful adaptation to its comic book roots.  
 
Some of the big highlights in this game, is how this games flows like an interactive movie done right with some solid shooting mechanics and unique darkness powers which are fun to mess around with. The narrative is remarkably strong exploring Jackie’s guilt and flashback, while exploring themes regarding mental health subtly and the price of vengeance. What was surprising for me was its emphasis Jackie’s deteriorating mental state, well-paced story and for hard-core darkness fans, you are in for a treat.  There is an upgrading tree system and the usual formula of the darkness gaining its powers from dark corridors is still a blast to use. Shooting is tight and the gunplay does feel impactful but using the darkness powers all at the same time is immensely fun.  Slashing and throwing your minion at your enemies as you unleash a hail of bullets is a glory good time. 
 
The only downside here is the replay value thus recommending to get it when its on sale. There is not much, once you are done with the story that is about it. There is a four player co-op multiplayer which I have yet to try but for some reason it does not really draw me in. At the end of the day, I think the one thing I can take away from playing Darkness 2 was it was great movie to be immersed in.

The Darkness is an awesome hidden gem that deserves more recognition. While it might not have been a blockbuster hit, it offers a unique and engaging experience that still holds up well today. One thing I highly recommend is playing the game with a controller—some of the mouse and keyboard controls, particularly the melee attacks, can feel a bit clunky and awkward to pull off. Using a controller really smooths out the gameplay and makes combat feel more fluid and intuitive.

Visually, the game has aged remarkably well, thanks largely to its distinctive comic book-inspired art style. The graphics aren’t about hyper-realism, but the bold, stylized visuals give The Darkness a striking, memorable look that sets it apart from other shooters and action games. The combination of gritty urban environments and supernatural elements creates a dark, atmospheric world that pulls you in.

The story is gripping too, with a noir-style narrative that blends crime drama and supernatural horror in a way few games manage to pull off. The protagonist’s internal struggle and the dark powers he wields add layers of depth to the gameplay, making it more than just another shooter.

Despite all these strengths, fans have been waiting a long time for a sequel. The Darkness 3 would be a welcome continuation of the story, and given the success of the first two games, it feels like the perfect time to revive the series.

If you’re looking for a game that combines intense action with a unique aesthetic and story, The Darkness is definitely worth playing—especially with a controller in hand.

The Darkness 2 is one of my personal favourites in a long list of games on my steam account. It is everything you could possibly want from a first person shooter that has a noire feeling to it, with light horror elements and an interesting story that will keep you hooked.

The story, without spoiling anything, is a direct sequel for the first part, meaning eveything ties up and the timelines are logical. Basically: you are Jackie Estacado, a young mafia member with dark powers beyond control,that seeks vengeance.The plot gets better and makes more sense as you play through the game. You have choices, tough it's not a primary element of the game and the story and levels are rather linear, choices only representing the question "do you want one more cutscene?", most of the times.

The gameplay is where this game really excels at. You have the basic fps mechanics with a strong emphasis on the signature dual wield of Jackie, which can carry 3 weapons with him- a primary, a secondary and another secondary, with the option to dual the secondaries or carefully aim with them. Besides that, the power of the darkness system is truly a breath of fresh air for the genre. Jackie has, at all times, 2 demon arms besides him that, if controlled right, can do huge amounts of damage just on their own. Tactically combined with the generic fps mechanics, they can adapt to any situation and turn the tides of battle in a second with specific skills. They can slash, execute enemies in exchange for health, ammo, etc, grab objects from the enviroment to use them as either defense or gory offense. Your godly powers go away in the light tough, as the game offers dynamic light gameplay elements, requiring you to think strategically before encounters as you shoot lights out and cut down heads.

The game also has a skill tree system, featuring 4 different skill trees that all branch out from a primary ability and that can be leveled simultaneously. The primary skill adds a new mechanic, eating the hearts of enemies (dead ones, of course) and replinishing health by it and gaining more points towards the purchase of your next skill. Every skill tree has a speciality and any skill you get can drastically change the gameplay and your methods of brutally murdering bad guys, making the end game the most fun of all, as you got so many tools in your arsenal that every situation is your playground. The skills you get also scale with your own, as you learn to further multitask the demon arms while still keeping concentrated on the basic firefights and making the ultimate killing machine out of you. That's why even the hardest difficulty doesn't feel unfair in any way, but challenging and forcing you to sharpen those reflexes make use of everything you learn. It's a masterpiece to be quite honest with you. 

Just so you can get the idea of how deep this game can be (story-wise), before the TL;DR, I'll leave you with my favourite monologue of Jackie Estacado: "Time slips away from you. And then, all of a sudden, it's like you're sitting in a theatre, watching a movie of your own life. You're a fu**ing movie star. And you're killing all the bad guys-tearing them limb from limb.And you feel good, you look good. F**k, you ARE good. And then you realize something: everyone else in the theatre? They're screaming, because they're watching a horror movie...and you're not the hero...you're the monster..."

As a fan of the original, this game is overall a huge disappointment. 

The TL;DR of this review is solid 5/10, continue on for the reasons.

Let's list some of the pros first though
Pros: The game is so short, you won't lose any of your life playing it.

Darkness powers are varied in a way, by adding nice neat little passive bonuses or effects that amp them up somewhat. Swarm joins the fray as a new power, and demon arm is no longer a proper power, rather just a flailing melee attack. The guns do not return, but are replaced by gun channeling. 

Gunplay is fairly solid, ammo will feel a bit tight at times if you aren't hitting your shots or using the darkness, though sometimes you'll question how a shot was a miss.

The relics are pretty neat, great little bits of extra story and listening to the narration will reveal touchs of dialogue that aren't written on the description.

Enemy variety is up, to present a challange not present in the original. Where as the original was almost entirely just shooty gun dudes, this game introduces Teleporting, Armored, and Shielded enemies, who can present just enough challange to make the combat interesting to a degree.

Now for the cons
Cons: The game is so short, you'll wonder why your wallet let you buy it
While gunplay is solid, the guns themselves are not. The original had fewer guns overall but the guns felt varied, instead of just "Stronger version of previous gun" 

The powers were much more satisfying in the original game, the Dark Guns for example were a blast to use, and black hole was destructive without just being a 'End current skirmish' button. Possessing the head was fun, and I'm sad to see it hasn't returned in this game, the darkling is a close replacement but he can't climb on the walls (Why can darkling no longer climb walls?)

Story is a little bland really, most interesting part was the horrible asylum parts. No real side missions like in the original (Harmonica guy's storyline while brief had Jackie's best line in the game). You learn a bit about the new guys in the game in what little inbetween time you had, though that is limited to the safe house, no roaming a small sect of areas as you please, exploring this and that. There is a little bit you can do (Shooting with Dolfo) which isn't so bad, but since you don't really spend any time getting to know anyone, it makes certain moments like the [spoiler] Sacrifical choice between Frank and Ed [/spoiler] lackluster. I only felt anything regarding [spoiler] Aunt Sarah	[/spoiler] because I knew them from the first game.

Enemy variety, while listed as a pro, is also a con, because with all of the new enemies, you can just whip your arm at them as you please until they die. The enemy variety was pretty stagnant in the first game, but since demon arm was a power, it had to recharge, so you couldn't just flail about and cross your fingers that they die, you had to actually hit the enemy.

Hardly any collectibles unlike the original. No funny phone calls to make, no letters to mail that would net you some concept art or such (Some issues of the darkness comic book, for example). While the relics are as stated neat due to how indepth they are, they're just added to keep the game from being a bland shooter that would only stand out because you have powers. In the original, the collectibles weren't glowing and grabbable by the arms, so you had to actually find them by their faint shine and going out of your way to look for them.

'Boss fights' Were alright, though definately lacking what it felt fighting the giant beast or even the fight with the Darkness itself. Even killing the 'Final boss' felt pretty lackluster compared to when you kill Uncle Paulie. 

Dipped into the new co-op, which was alright, the characters are fairly unique,  though with no real unique power of their own, just borrowing from Jackie, they did have unique weapons, which I liked a fair amount. 

The lack of the multiplayer that The Darkness had is a minor disappointment, the original multiplayer was fairly fun, especially switching between human and darkling form, making use of the darkling's exceptional mobility to ambush someone in your human form was  execellent. I'm not holding this against the Darkness II, just lamenting that it isn't in the game.

Anyway, overall, I wasn't too pleased with this game, and I don't expect to replay it anytime soon, compared to the original, which I've played through multiple times.

[b]-----Update on 13 Oct, 2025-----[/b]

Nightdive Studios mentioned a year ago that they planned to remaster The Darkness and port it to PC, but nothing has happened since. Tired of waiting, I decided to play the original game.

Using an emulator, the game ran smoothly with my Xbox controller, while the keyboard had camera issues. I’m not used to controllers, at first I struggled even on Easy difficulty. When I discovered the auto-aim mechanic it got better, just raise the gun near an enemy, and the cursor will automatically lock onto them. All I need to do is a slight adjustment upward to ensure a headshot.

The biggest difference between The Darkness and The Darkness II is the use of the Darkness powers. In the first game, during my 3 hours of play, Jackie has the Darkness power but can’t directly control it to attack. Instead, he relied on pistols or rifles. In contrast, The Darkness II lets Jackie fully wield the Darkness as a powerful killing tool.

The Darkness tentacles are primarily used for puzzles in the first game. It moves like a snake, climbing walls or slipping through vents to reach areas on the other side to unlock a door. You can also summon a minion (similar to those in Overlord) to assist in combat.

For the story, Darkness I reveals that the Darkness found Jackie on his 21st birthday, which is a curse passed down from his great great grandfather, who seems to be fighting in WWII at the moment. Jackie left Jenny in the orphanage and is now entangled in the family’s criminal business. The story unfolds across NYCity, with authentic details like the subway station, including real stops like Fulton Avenue and realistic exit turnstiles.

However, the game’s direction is poor. I often felt lost, especially at the WWII level. I was lucky to find the bunker, unlock it with a minion, and progress toward the second crucifix, but got completely lost and stuck in the end.

After wandering aimlessly, I gave up. Despite this, The Darkness remains a great game in its genre, still playable with some impressive visuals. I’ve heard there’s a plot twist, but I’ll need to pick up the game later or watch a walkthrough on YouTube. I hope Nightdive Studios delivers the remaster or Darkness III someday.

I’ve been sitting on this review for a while as I don’t fully know how to approach it.

Let me start by saying this game took me by surprise.  I had prepared myself for a fairly generic shooter with some cool monster abilities.  What I hadn’t expected was the absolutely terrific presentation and story.  The more I think on my time with this game, the more impressed I am by it.

Jackie is a distraught human suffering from his own power.  He knows he’s the bad guy, that he hurts those around him.  Slowly spiraling downwards as he desperately tries to cling to those he loves.  He needs to stop the cycle of violence in himself, to stop trying to control everything through force.  But he can’t, he doesn’t know any other way.  He was made to do this.

They could have so easily phoned it in and just made him a raging badass with no character and the game would be okay.  It’d get the job done.  But the fact they took so much time to make him a compelling, well rounded character, brings the game from an above average shooter to one of the best in its genre.  What helps is the writers aren’t afraid to take you out of the action for character development.  They plop you into a mental asylum for half the game to build on its themes.  To make you question what is and isn’t real.  In terms of writing it’s no Red Dead or Bioshock but it’s still really bloody good.

And the gameplay isn’t half bad either.  The gunplay is fine, nothing to write home about but it is elevated by the monster's abilities.  You can melee and bite and what have you, which is fine but it has the usual problem with these types of games where shooting the enemy is just the most efficient way to deal with them.  That is, except for one attack.  The ol’ gravity gun.

You can throw almost any prop on the map at your enemies.  This can range from small bricks all the way to literal spears that impale people against walls.  It’s as simple as picking it up and throwing it, making it flow into combat very easily.  And there is a heavy incentive to use it as it can be done while shooting.  It seems like such a little thing to add but it makes the gameplay so much more dynamic and just plain fun.  Even when the game starts to drag its feet near the middle it's still just fun.  You are also constantly finding new, better weapons and since you run out of ammo pretty quick you have to pick up new ones.  Forcing you to change tactics on the fly.  Making for an excellent shooter.

Well, you might say, it seems like you really enjoyed it.  So why is it hard to approach?

That’s because it stands as a great game, one of the best I’ve played this year.  But it’s not great in terms of all the great games I’ve played.  Let me rephrase this.  If I had a tier list, of all the games I’d ever played, I’d put this in at the top of B tier.  This might sound like a dis to the game but really I mean it as praise.

For movies, something like Citizen Kane can easily stand up to later movies like Blade Runner 2049, it can all be placed on the same line.  A game like The Darkness will never be able to stand up to a game like Red Dead II or Cyberpunk.  It just can’t.  The scope of each of these games, no matter how great The Darkness II is, will never be able to match these games in quality.

This should not lessen the impact nor artistic merit of this game.  I need to emphasize that it stands at the top of its respected category.  It falls behind games like Metro and Half-Life, though depending on who you ask it would probably do better than Metro (that’s purely my own biased opinion), but it does way better than games like Crysis, AvP, Amnesia, and FEAR.  It threatens to leak into A tier. It's so well made.

And that’s okay.  It’s not trying to be a masterpiece.  It’s not trying to be this huge open ended game with ludacris amounts of detail and tons to do.  It’s a linear, story driven, midtier FPS and it owns it.  It knows what it is and it damn near perfects it.

Oh except for the multiplayer, don’t go anywhere near that.

8/10 - A game could have been a by the books shooter, but chose to be better, maybe even the best.  For all smaller scale shooters this is my new benchmark that all games of its nature should aspire to be.

The Darkness II is what happens when someone hands you a Tommy gun, two demonic tentacles, and politely asks you to please resolve your mafia problems through extreme overkill.

You play as Jackie Estacado, a mob boss who also happens to be the host of an ancient demon called The Darkness. The result? A game where you can shoot enemies, impale them with demon arms, rip car doors off to use as shields, and then feed hearts to your eldritch buddy for dessert. Subtlety is not on the menu.

Compared to the moody, grounded first game, Darkness II goes full comic book—literally. The cel-shaded art style makes it feel like you’re playing a living graphic novel, complete with gory executions that are equal parts brutal and hilarious. (There’s just something about using a tentacle to rip a guy in half like wet cardboard that never gets old.)

The story is surprisingly heartfelt, too. Jackie is still haunted by the loss of his girlfriend Jenny, and the game leans hard into themes of grief, trauma, and whether the real curse is the demon inside him… or the empty apartment without her. It’s cheesy noir mixed with bloody chaos, and it works.

Add in your little Darkling sidekick (imagine Gollum in a Union Jack shirt with a love for urinating on corpses), and you’ve got one of the most unique shooters of its generation.

This review is based on 100% completion and 11.5 hours of gameplay, with many more on Xbox.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend the game? Absolutely. I have a nostalgic attachment from playing this years ago on Xbox, but I enjoyed it then, and I definitely enjoyed it now. It’s refreshing to play a simple FPS without over-the-top mechanics or inserted politics. You play as a mobster with some powers, and that’s exactly what you get. Note that this game has many adult themes, but it’s all part of the experience, which is just fun overall.

Starting with the sound design and audio, I thought it was all excellent—the voice acting was solid, the music was good, and the in-game sounds were crisp. However, the startup sound is inexplicably loud, blasting even when my speakers were set low. Unfortunately, there doesn’t seem to be a way to adjust it that I could find, so be prepared for a loud startup intro. Thankfully, you can skip it quickly by pressing any button.

The gameplay is really good and straightforward, which was refreshing. The gunplay is solid, and the abilities slot easily into the experience. I personally preferred dual-wielding and the run-and-gun style rather than the two-handed weapons, which felt a bit lacking, even on a  lower difficulty. Overall, though, it’s a great shooter.

The narrative is also well done and easy to follow. While it’s fairly short, it does a good job presenting a dark, gritty story with adult themes, much like an old mafia or mobster film. The campaign is a very solid experience, and the only bug I ran into involved getting stuck while controlling the Darkling or crawling through tight spaces. Turning on V-sync fixed it for me, and while you may still get stuck occasionally, jumping around usually lets you pass through.

Aside from the campaign, the game also includes Vendetta and Hit List modes, which serve as its multiplayer/co-op experiences. You can play these solo [i](though a couple of Hit List missions are co-op-only)[/i], and they’re essentially side missions that add a bit more content. While they’re not spectacular, they’re okay for a bit of extra gameplay.

Since this is an older game, it goes on sale frequently, so if you can wait, I’d recommend grabbing it on discount. If you can’t wait, it’s still worth trying even at full price.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
The 100% completion was fun for me, as I just like the game. I recommend doing two playthroughs: one on easy to complete everything at a relaxed pace, and one on the hardest difficulty for a quick sprint to tidy up anything missed and pick up the last difficulty achievements.

There’s an excellent Steam guide by Cynic 0055 and Kestrel 0010, which provides a thorough step-by-step guide for the achievements. Which you can check out [b][url= https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2234749410] here. [/url][/b]

Overall, the achievements are pretty easy, and the guide makes them even simpler. They include kill achievements, collectables, story-related unlocks, and some from the multiplayer mode, which can be done solo. Completing the main campaign achievements should take around 9–10 hours. My first playthrough on easy, focusing on collectables and kill achievements, took 6 hours, while speeding through on the hardest difficulty only took just under 3. Fortunately, you can skip a lot of cutscenes and dialogue, so it’s definitely faster the second time around.

The Vendetta and Hit List achievements are also straightforward—just play through on Thug difficulty, and you’ll breeze through. Although these are co-op/multiplayer modes, they’re all able to be done solo.
